prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: My opening ranking placed IceCube first, and I have reconsidered it after reading the full set of ballots. Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the candidate with the broadest and most robust support across the committee: six of seven rankers put it in their top three and three put it first, and the supporting arguments are about the science, not about popularity. It is a rare case in which a specific quantitative theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of flat bands at a magic angle) was followed years later by an experimental discovery (correlated insulators and superconductivity, Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators, 2018) that opened a new field. Many independent laboratories reproduced the phenomenology within a few years and extended it to other moire platforms, and the tuning parameter, the twist angle, is a genuinely new experimental knob. The theory plus experiment trio maps onto the credited names without strain, and the work has not yet been recognised by an earlier prize, although the 2016 topological-phases prize and the 2010 graphene prize are neighbouring context rather than overlap.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity of the interpretation. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved, device-to-device twist-angle disorder complicates comparisons, and the field is only about eight years old, so a prize now would rest on the platform and the observation of correlated phases rather than a settled mechanism. Attribution is also incomplete: the three names cannot represent the first-author experimental work, earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, or the many groups that later established fractional Chern and other states. Finally, as an experimentalist I am aware that my own field's candidate (IceCube, B016) is the one I am setting aside; I do not want that to look like deference to a majority, and I record that the maturity concern above would be a reason to wait if the committee thinks the field needs a few more years.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B038 first as a prediction matched by nature, but flags that early twisted-graphene theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) and the experimental first author are not in the credited set, and that the unsettled pairing mechanism may affect the citation.
responses.response: I agree with the value placed on a quantitative prediction confirmed by experiment, and I agree the early-theory question is real. I would answer it by anchoring the citation to the two things that are decisive and uniquely quantitative, the 2011 flat-band prediction at the magic angle and the 2018 observation of correlated and superconducting states, and by phrasing it so that it does not claim a mechanism. The earlier continuum-model work of Lopes dos Santos and colleagues treated the twist but did not predict the flat-band magic angle with the interaction-driven consequences, which is where I would draw the line. I cannot fully rule out that other members will weigh the priority history differently, and I am relying on the ballots, not on an independent check.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory first for its lasting impact on correlated-electron theory, but acknowledges that omitting Metzner, who introduced the infinite-dimension limit with Vollhardt, is a genuine fairness concern.
responses.response: I take the scientific weight of DMFT seriously and I do not equate my lower ranking of it with lower merit; it is simply outside my own expertise. But I think Eriksson's own caveat is close to disqualifying under the supplied credits: a prize that has to omit Metzner while crediting Vollhardt for the same limit is difficult to defend, and Mehlig notes that Nobel recognition of methods is rare and that the validation is approximate in finite dimensions. The twisted-graphene case shares an open mechanism question, but it has a discrete, falsifiable observation and a clean attribution, which DMFT lacks on the supplied evidence. I would welcome a clearer argument for how the three DMFT names could be defended.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first for its architectural impact on superconducting processors, noting that the 2025 prize already recognised macroscopic quantum effects in circuits and that Girvin cannot be added to the credited trio.
responses.response: The impact of circuit QED is not in doubt, and I accept that reproducibility and independent confirmation are stronger there than in the moire case. My reservation is the one Johansson himself raises: with the 2025 prize on circuit quantum effects so recent, and the 2004 proposal credited to five people of whom only three can be named, a follow-on award is harder to justify now than a prize in a platform that has not been recognised at all. I also note that Johansson works in this area, as he says, which is a reason to weigh his enthusiasm carefully but not to discount his scientific argument. I keep B026 outside my preferred configuration and would not object to revisiting it later.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first, arguing that Katori's magic-wavelength idea plus Ye's record accuracy form a clean two-person prize, mature and confirmed independently across laboratories, with the redefinition of the second under discussion.
responses.response: I agree that B045 is mature, cleanly attributed and a strong candidate; I ranked it fifth and have kept it as an alternative for exactly those reasons. Where I qualify the case is novelty relative to the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, since lattice clocks build directly on both and, as Danielsson observes, the committee may regard the achievement as invention of an instrument and not a discovery. I would also hold that the redefinition of the second is a metrology decision still in the future, not evidence of scientific merit. If the committee prefers a precision-measurement prize this year, I would support it as a fallback, but I do not think it displaces the moire discovery on originality.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B038 first and B023 second, treating topological insulators as deep and overdue but noting that the credited set omits Mele, Bernevig, Zhang and Hasan and that the quantum anomalous Hall part may need separate treatment.
responses.response: I agree that the topological-insulator science is overdue and that the field is mature, and I ranked B023 seventh mainly because of the attribution problem Mehlig himself identifies, since the entry mixes quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall discoveries and leaves out Mele, whose work with Kane is inseparable. I think the committee should not try to rescue this by combining pieces of B023 and B040 into a configuration the supplied credits do not support. I would value Mehlig's view on whether a two-part prize pairing a topological-insulator achievement with the moire one is defensible, because I judge that the three-person limit makes it unworkable without cutting a key name from B038.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the unsettled superconducting pairing mechanism as a reason to defer B038, or accepts the platform and correlated-state discovery as sufficient.

Whether the citation should credit only the 2011 prediction and 2018 experiments, or whether earlier twisted-bilayer theory and the first-author experimental contributions require a wording that acknowledges them.

Whether IceCube (B016) is better recognised now on the diffuse-flux detection or deferred until source identification matures, and how large-collaboration credit among Halzen, Karle and other leaders should be handled.
I am working from the ballots and my recollection of the priority history, not from an independent check.
statement.conflict_note: I am an astroparticle experimentalist on PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, and the IceCube candidate (B016) is in my own broad field, so I would recuse myself from the final decision on B016 if it came to a vote, even though my profile documents no direct link to IceCube or to its credited individuals. No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B038, B045 or the other shortlisted candidates.
